note: (Shein, Wilson, Larin, Wurtman) McLean Hosp. Res. Lab., Belmont, MA, United States
title: Stimulation of [14C]serotonin synthesis from [ 14C]tryptophan by mescaline in rat pineal organ cultures
abstract: Addition of mescaline to the nutrient medium of rat pineal glands in organ culture produces a marked increase in pineal synthesis of serotonin from [ 14C] tryptophan. By contrast, addition of psilocybin or lysergic acid diethylamide (LDS) has no effect on [14C] serotonin synthesis by these cultures. Mescaline has no effect on pineal [14C] serotonin synthesis when [14C] 5 hydroxytryptophan is substituted for [ 14C] tryptophan as the labelled substrate. Mescaline does not inhibit the deamination of [14C] serotonin to 5 hydroxyindoleacetic acid and has no significant effect on the intracellular content of [14C] tryptophan or its conversion to [14C] protein. It is concluded that mescaline stimulates pineal [14C] serotonin synthesis via a primary stimulatory action on the enzymatic conversion of [14C] tryptophan to 5 hydroxytryptophan, rather than by effects on other steps in the indole pathway or on cellular uptake of [14C] tryptophan.

author_address: B.S. Meldrum, MRC Neuropsychiat. Unit, Carshalton
note: (Meldrum, Naquet) MRC Neuropsychiat. Unit, Carshalton
title: Effects of psilocybin, dimethytaryptamine, mescaline and various lysergic acid derivates on the eeg and on photically induced epilepsy in the baboon (papio papio)
abstract: Following the demonstration that iysergide (LSD) inhibits myoclonic responses to intermittent photic stimulation (ILS) in the baboon, some other hallucinogenic drugs and some 'nonhallucinogenic' derivatives of lysergic acid have been tested for their effects on the EEG and on photically induced epilepsy in 22 adolescent baboons (Papio papio). Psilocybine (1 to 4 mg/kg) and dimethyltryptamine (2 to 4 mg/kg) produced marked autonomie effects, EEG changes consistent with a severe disturbance of consciousness and a complete abolition of myoclonic or paroxysmal EEG responses to ILS (thus closely resembling the effect of LSD, 40 to 100 pg/kg). Mescaline (up to 32 mg/kg) was relatively ineffective on both the background EEG and on the myoclonic responses to ILS. After methysergide (2 to 5 mg/kg), although the autonomie effects were less severe than after psilocybine, there were muscular hypotonie, an abnormal EEG and reduction or abolition of the epileptic responses to ILS. Bromolysergide and methergoline appeared less potent than methysergide, but, at 4 mg/kg, both drugs abolished ILS induced myoclonus. Averaged responses to flash stimulation showed that psilocybine resembled LSD 25 in modifying transmission in the afferent visual pathway, whereas methysergide, in doses blocking ILS induced myoclonus, did not alter primary evoked responses in the visual cortex. It is suggested that a serotoninergic system is probably involved in the epileptic responses of the baboon to ILS.

author_address: J. Kolarik, Inst. Higher Nerv. Activity, Med. Fac., Palacky Univ., Olomouc
note: (Kolarik) Inst. Higher Nerv. Activity, Med. Fac., Palacky Univ., Olomouc
title: Eeg changes after psilocybin in organic brain lesions
abstract: A study was made of the effect of psilocybine in a mean dose of 0.16 mg/kg on the EEG picture in 54 subjects with organic brain lesions of various localization and etiology, mostly verified neurosurgically. Results: the most typical finding after psilocybine was a desynchronization in 79.6% of patients (in 100% of parietal lobe lesions, in 801 of frontal lobe lesions, in 75% of temporal lobe lesions and in 33.3% of occipital lobe lesions). The desynchronization after psilocybine was of a peculiar character in the EEG with focal and diffuse pathologic activity. The extent and intensity of the slow activity were most suppressed in frontal and parietal lesions, and to a lesser extent in temporal and occipital lesions. The psychotomimetic effects of psilocybine correlated with the EEG desynchronization. The hallucinogenic effect was absent in 90.9% of cases without desynchronization following psilocybine. The visual hallucinogenic effect and EEG desynchronization (Kolarik et al. 1966) were least frequent in occipital lobe lesions. In occipital lesions suppression of EEG reactivity was the greatest (alpha blocking reaction and photostimulation). Diffuse epileptic activity of subcortical origin was strongly suppressed by psilocybine, while conversely focal primary cortical epileptic activity increased in several recordings depending upon the degree of desynchronization, especially in parietofrontal lesions. Four functional levels within the CNS are considered from which a generalized desynchronization could be evoked: (1) The level of the pontine reticular formation whose significance is made evident in the studies of rhombencephalic sleep. (2) The level of the reticular ascending activating system (RAAS). Most authors assume that hallucinogenic drugs act precisely at this level of the brain stem reticular formation. (3) The functional depression of the recruiting system at the level of the medial thalamus (Monnier 1959). (4) Hyperexcitability of the cortical neurons after psilocybine. The highest values of psilocybine were found in the neocortex, thalamus and certain layers of the hippocampus whilst the values were low in the hypothalamus, the nuclei of the socalled extrapyramidal motor system and the reticular formation.

title: Different reaction of focal and diffuse epileptic eeg activity to psilocybin
abstract: In 30 epileptic patients the influence of psilocybine (average dose 0.16 mg/kg) on the epiletic EEG tracing was studied. Before the adinistration of psilocybine (Ps) pathologic EEG changes were present in all 30 patients. Ps provoked a generalized EEG desynchronization in 90% (27 patients). Focal epileptic activity (present in 70% i.e. 21 patients before Ps) increased after Ps in 23.3% (7 patients) and remained unchanged or was attenuated in 46.6% (14 patients). Diffuse epileptic activity present in 63.3% (i.e. 17 patients) before Ps persisted in only 101 (3 patients) after Ps. Diffuse epileptic activity of subcortical origin was most strongly suppressed by Ps (a decreased incidence of paroxysmal bilateral synchronous spike and wave complexes as well as of interparoxysmal continuous diffuse slow activity, and other subcortical discharges of a different etiology). Desynchronization occuired in 100% of parietal lobe lesions, in 80% of frontal lobe lesions, in 75% of temporal lobe lesions and in 33.3% of occipital lobe lesions (Kolarik 1967). The incidence of focal epileptic activity after Ps was similar: it was most frequent in parietal lobe lesions (751 in comparison with 62.5% before Ps), and was noted in 50% of frontal lobe lesions, in 37.5% of temporal lobe lesions and only in 33.3% of occipital lobe lesions. It is suggested that hyperexcitability of cortical neurons (Gastaut 1953) produced by Ps is analogous with their pathologic irritability giving rise to the focal epileptic manifestations. The role of the depression of the mediothalamic recruiting system after Ps as demonstrated experimentally by Monnier (1959) and its special action in 2 opposing directions is noteworthy. On the one hand, simultaneously with the depression of the recruiting system the subcortical epileptic activities and other slow wave activities, subcortical in origin, are suppressed. On the other hand, the depression of the recruiting system localizes cortical desynchronization predominantly in a frontoparietal recruiting system (Whitteridge and Walsh 1963), thus accentuating the focal epileptic activity in this localization. This may be due not only to the induction of cortical excitation by the depression of the mediothalamic recruiting system but also to a direct exciting effect of psilocybine on cortical elements.

journal_name: Comptes rendus des seances de la Societe de biologie et de ses filiales
title: Modifications of sound and light conditioning of evoked responses in man by psilocybine
abstract: The effect of psilocybine on sensory conditioning was studied in 13 subjects (39 tests). During conditioning a sound which originally had little effect induced a marked and stable evoked response in the occipital area when coupled with light. The drug caused disappearance of this established conditioning, the potentials evoked by the conditioned sound becoming less marked and less stable. It also induced a new type of acquisition as reflected by the appearance of slow, late, marked and generalized phenomena provoked by the conditioned sound. These phenomena reproduced the aspect of the slow waves evoked by light (unconditional stimulus) after ingestion of psilocybine. These changes were very similar to the responses observed after conditioning to sound and light in psychotic children. This similarity provides an electrophysiological evidence for relationships between drug induced and clinical psychosis.

title: Psilocybin induced contraction of nearby visual space
abstract: Using apparent fronto parallel plane (AFP) monitoring techniques, the relative stability of the abut hic plane, i.e. Euclidean visual space, was investigated in 16 volunteers with a median age of 23.5 y r under 160/ig/kg psilocybin induced ergotropic arousal. Handwriting area and pressure were also measured in the same subjects. Dru, induced contraction of nearby visual space was interred from changes of AFP curvature and tilt, as well as from increased handwriting area at drug peak. The 'rising horizon' (Rentiert) in the drawings of schizophrenics is also considered a manifestation of the contraction of visual space and is described in terms of an arousal dependent transformation of constancies. The 'projection' of central nervous system activity as experience out there' is also discussed as an arousal dependent learned constancy.

author_address: N.W. Scholes, Dept. Physiol. Pharmacol., Sch. Veter. Med., Univ. California, Davis, Calif. 95616
note: (Scholes, Gutnick) Dept. Physiol. Pharmacol., Sch. Veter. Med., Univ. California, Davis, Calif. 95616
title: Relative activity of psychotoxic drugs on the avian optic lobe
abstract: Because of restriction in the use of psychotoxic (psychotomimetic) drugs in the human, a subhuman experimental tool suitable for the study of these drugs and their antagonists would be useful. Using standard electraphysiological techniques, the action of psychotoxic drugs on the electrical activity of the optic tectum of the young chick has been studied. The i.v. administration of lysergide to this animal produces a well defined and consistent change in tectal activity. A comparable change occurs following administration of other psychotomimetic agents (psilocybin, mescaline and amphetamine). The relative potency of these agents on tectal activity compares favorably with their relative psychotoxic potency in man. These results favor the view that the mechanism of action of these psychotomimetic agents on the chick tectum resembles, to some degree, their psychotoxic properties in man. It is suggested that the avian preparation may be useful for the study of the pharmacology of psychotoxic drugs and antagonists.

tertiary_title: Etude des effets ei.ectrophysiologiques de la psilocybine chez un cercopithecinae, papio papio
author_address: F. Bermond, Lab. de Neurobiol, Fac. de Med., Dakar
note: (Bermond, Bert) Lab. de Neurobiol, Fac. de Med., Dakar
title: Electrophysiologic effects of psilocybin in a baboon, papio papio
abstract: The electrophysiological effects of psilocybin were studied in baboons (Papio papio). The visual response was studied by ERG and by lateral geniculate body and visual cortex evoked potentials. The primary visual cortex evoked potentials are the only ones to show significant constant and long lasting modifications. The effects on somaesthetic evoked potentials are weak, inconsistent and most often chatacterized by a slight decrease in amplitude. Psilocybin has no durable effect on the EEG. A specific activity of psilocybin on the visual primary cortex may be considered as the basis of hallucinatory phenomena induced in man by this drug.

author_address: Div. of Exp. Pharmacol., Inst. of Physiol., Univ. of Glasgow
note: (Sugrue) Div. of Exp. Pharmacol., Inst. of Physiol., Univ. of Glasgow
title: A study of the role of noradrenaline in behavioural changes produced in the rat by psychotomimetic drugs
abstract: LSD 25, psilocybin and JB 329 reduced the noradrenaline content of the rat hypothalamus. All 3 drugs affected the acquisition of a conditioned avoidance response, LSD 25 and psilocybin retarding and JB 329 enhancing the acquisition. With the exception of JB 329, doses affecting the acquisition of a conditioned avoidance response were lower than those required to decide hypothalamic noradrenaline concentrations. The time of peak drug effect on the acquisition of a conditioned avoidance response occurred approximately 1.5 hr after injection as opposed to 3 hr in the case of noradrenaline content The amount of LSD 25, psilocybin and JB 329 necessary to elicit gross behavioral excitation was similar to the dose producing noradrenaline depletion. Here also peak behavioral effect was detected earlier. Pretreatment with reserpine and alpha MT had no effect on the intensity of gross behavioral excitation induced by LSD 25 and psilocybin but shortened the duration of the response. The excitation induced by JB 329 was abolished by reserpine pretreatment and was markedly reduced both in intensity and duration by the prior injection of alpha MT.

author_address: E.T. Uyeno, Stanford Res. Inst., Menlo Park, CA, United States
note: (Uyeno) Stanford Res. Inst., Menlo Park, CA, United States
title: Alteration of a learned response of the squirrel monkey by hallucinogens
abstract: The relative effectiveness of N,N dimethyltryptamine derivatives and amphetamine derivatives was evaluated in seven squirrel monkeys, trained to discriminate between 2 black discs of different sizes. After the animals learned the task, they were injected intraperitoneally with the test compounds and then retested. The dose response curves showed that debilitating effects of the compounds were a function of dose. The median effective doses (ED50) that disrupted their performance were calculated according to the graphic logarithmic probit method. The descendingrank order of effectiveness of the compounds, according to the ED50 was: 4 ethyl 2,5 dimethoxy amphetamine; 2,5 dimethoxy 4 methylamphetamine; psilocybin; 4 methoxy N1N dimethyltryptamine; N,N dimethyltryptamine; and 6 hydroxy N,N dimethyltryptamine.

author_address: M.A. Hockey, Div. of Behav. Scis, Dept. of Psychiat., Coll. of Med., Ohio State Univ., Columbus
note: (Hockey) Div. of Behav. Scis, Dept. of Psychiat., Coll. of Med., Ohio State Univ., Columbus
title: The influence of personality structure on the final result of model psychoses
abstract: With psylocybin an experimental psychotic condition could be induced in 15 volunteers and evaluated by the Minnesota Multiphasic Personality Inventory (MMPI), among which also the 2 reaction types occurred called exogenous and endogenous by Bonhoeffer's terminology. The degree of retest variability in the taste threshold value without any drug depends on the personality structure. The individual personality structure decisively determines reaction form, intensity, and final result of the psychosis.

title: The effect of psilocybin on the behavior of the cercopithecinae papiopapio
abstract: The effect of Psilocybin on the behavior of the baboon Papiopapio has been studied. Animal watchfulness, as estimated from the E. E. G., is enhanced within the first 5 minutes after injection and then is not further modified. Psilocybin induces a decrease of spontaneous motility. Conversely, the frequency of eye movements is considerably increased. This pattern might be explained by alterations of visual perception. au.

author_address: S.J. Mule, NIMH, Addict Res. Cent, Lexington, KY, United States
note: (Mule) NIMH, Addict Res. Cent, Lexington, KY, United States
title: Identification of narcotics, barbiturates, amphetamines, tranquilizers and psychotomimetics in human urine
abstract: This study was undertaken to evaluate the ion exchange paper technique and rapid direct extraction methods for obtaining drugs of abuse from urine and the subsequent identification of these drugs or metabolites by thin layer chromatography coupled with sequential chemical reagent spraving. Recoveries from urine +/-S.D. of 21.7 +/-5*A 2.4 +/-0.8e and 21 +/-were obtained for labeled morphine, pentobarbital and amphetamine, respectively, using the ion exchange paper technique. With this method most narcotic analgesics could be detected at a level of I pg/ml urine (50 ml urine sample). The method in general was unacceptable for detecting either barbiturates, amphetamines or certain psycho active drugs (psiloybin, glutethamide, chlorpromazine, marihuana). Percentage recoveries obtained with direct extraction from urine +/-S.D. were 61 +/-4degree4 for morphine Cu. 86 +/-SL for pentobarbital C14, and 61 +/- 21% for amphetamine H3. Utuiring direct extraction methods almost all the drugs of abuse could be detected at levels ranging from 1 to 2 /ig/uu of urine (15 ml of urine sample). The methods described in this report provided some specificity through differential pH extraction. The subsequent use of thin layer chromatography and sequential spray reagents allowed identification of specific drugs or metabolites. All methods and techniques could be completed within 24 h. The direct extraction in all cases and the ion exchange technique for narcotics were sufficiently sensitive to provide detection of drug usage 24 h after the last administration of drug. Both techniques were extremely simple to perform and did not require expensive equipment thus keeping the cost of analysis at a minimum. These techniques may readily be adapted to a urine monitoring program screening for drugs of abuse, provided the limitations as described are well understood.

author_address: F.J. Kane Jr., Dept. of Psychiat., Univ. of North Carolina, Chapel Hill, NC, United States
note: (Kane Jr., Keeler, Liptzin, Reifler) Dept. of Psychiat., Univ. of North Carolina, Chapel Hill, NC, United States
title: Hallucination of geometric forms associated with the use of sympatho mimetic agents
abstract: Three cases of acute paranoid psychosis with hallucination of colored geometric forms are reported associated with the use of sympathomimetic agents. No signs of organicity were present in these cases. These phenomena probably reflect alterations in neuronal activity in the retina as a result of the presence of central adrenergic stimulation. These phenomena have also been reported with other central adrenergic stimulants notably lysergide, psilocybine and mescaline.

note: (Hill, Fischer, Warshay) Coll. of Optom., Ohio State Univ., Columbus, OH 43210, United States
title: Effects of excitatory and tranquilizing drugs on visual perception. spatial distortion thresholds
abstract: The just perceptible degree of optically induced curvature of a horizontal black line was investigated in student volunteers under the influence of psilocybine. The drug produced a definite but transient loss of ability to compensate for the distortion.

author_address: R. Fischer, Dept. of Psychiat., Coll. of Med., Ohio State Univ., Columbus, OH 43210, United States
note: (Fischer, Hill, Warshay) Dept. of Psychiat., Coll. of Med., Ohio State Univ., Columbus, OH 43210, United States
title: Effects of the psychodysleptic drug psilocybin on visual perception. changes in brightness preference
abstract: In healthy young volunteers (students) psilocybine caused a reversible change in brightness preference. This change showed correlation to the personality characteristics of the subjects, but not to the mydriatic action of the drug.

journal_name: Psychopharmacol. - Nat. Inst. Ment. Hlth. Wash.
title: Relationships between the conformation of psychedelic drugs and their psychotropic potency
abstract: A review on structure activity relationships of drugs is useful as a tool in determining their mode of action and facilitating the development of more potent agents. Among the psychedelic drugs of the mescaline, LSD, psilocybin class, there are some dramatic variations in potency with small changes in chemical structure.

tertiary_title: Propklozeptlve slnnestauschumibn und akzentuiefhng hzw manifestwkrden neuroirgiscueii svmpixjmatik unter psilocybin bei hlrngeschadtoten versuchspersonen
author_address: B. Dubansky, Lab. fur Hohere Nerventatigkeit, Med. Fak., Palacky Univ., Olomouc
note: (Dubansky, Vyhnankova, Setlik) Lab. fur Hohere Nerventatigkeit, Med. Fak., Palacky Univ., Olomouc
title: Proprioceptive hallucinations and accentuation or manifestation of neurologic symptomatology after administration of psilocybine to persons with cerebral lesions
abstract: In view of the fact that proprioception, as a feedback component, is an integral factor in all forms of motor activity, and that propiioceptive hallucinations are, together with the optic stimulation syndrome, the commonest effects of psilocybine, an investigation of a possible correlation between proprioceptive hallucinations and motor performance was conducted with 99 patients having brain lesions of various etiology and localization. A single dose (0.15 mg/kg) of psilocybine was administered orally or s.c. The following neurological signs (percentage incidence in brackets) were evaluated in relation to the occurrence of proprioceptive hallucinations: Accentuation of paretic phenomena of central origin (84%); manifestation of paretic phenomena previously absent (45degree/); dysarthria (5Ti); accentuation ot some second signal disorders (disturbance of expressive speeck, amnestic aphasia, agraphia, apraxia, stereoagnosia) (68degree4); disorders of neuromuscular coordination (534); motor irritative phenomena such as tremor and myoclonus (2ffu) and provocation of epileptic phenomena (22degree4). Of 48 patients with accentuation of paretic signs, 39 (8) had proprioceptive sensations (significant correlation: x2corr. = 6.46; p< 0.05). For manifestation of paretic phenomena (16 of the 39 patients initially free from paresis) 14 of the patients had concomitant proprioceptive hallucinations (x2corr.=3.72; p<0.05). For accentuation or manifestation of dysarthria (x2=s3.17; p<0.05), for occurrence of coordination disturbances (x2=3.93; p < 0.05) and for deterioration of second signal phenomena related to motor activity (x2=5.29; p<0.05) the findings were similar. No statistically significant correlation be established between trc;vsui, epileptic phenomena etc. induced by psilocybine and the presence of proprioceptive hallucinations because the numbers were too small. Reference is made to other publications, and further studies, making use of electromyography, are proposed.

tertiary_title: Unterschiede in der reaktionsweise von psilocybin bei hibngeschadigten versuchspersonen bezogen auf die lokalisation der lasjon
author_address: B. Dubansky, Lab. fur Hohere Nerventatigkeit, Med. Fak., Pato.cky Univ., Olomouc
note: (Dubansky, Vyhnankova) Lab. fur Hohere Nerventatigkeit, Med. Fak., Pato.cky Univ., Olomouc
title: Differences in reaction after administration of psilocybin in persons suffering from cerebral lesions of different localization
abstract: The possibility of difference in susceptibility to psilocybine between normal subjects and patients with organic brain damage of various localizations was investigated. A single dose of 0.15 mg/kg psilocybine was given orally or s.c. to 99 patients and 12 normal subjects. It was already known that the effect of psychotomimetic (hallucinogenic) agents is appreciably less in brain damaged or psychotic patients than in normal persons; this was confirmed with psilocybine, especially as regards the optic stimulation syndrome. More detailed analysis showed that the reduced optic effect, and in most of these cases also the reduced total psychotomimetic effect, was to some degree correlated with the nature of the brain lesion, the presence of an elevated intracranial pressure and the age and sex of the patient. No influence of the administration route was discernible. A notable and statistically highly significant (chi2 32.71; p < 0.01) correlation was found between the reduced optic effect of psilocybine and the localization of the brain lesion. In patients with lesions of the occipital lobe and the adjacent temporal and parietal regions (33 persons), with clinical signs of a lesion of the central structures of the optic system (optic agnosia or hemianoptic visual field defects) the optical effect of psilocybine was present in only 24% as against B5'i of the patients with other brain lesions (this latter figure approximated closely the incidence of visual hallucinations in normal subjects). Differences in incidence of some qualitativelyUYUUUUIUUU different visual phenomena were also found. In patients with lesions of the central structures of the optic system, all components of the optic stimulation system were greatly reduced (entoptic phenomena; elementary and formed visions; complex (figurative and scenic) hallucinations and dysmegaloptic and dysmorphoptic disturbances), in comparison with the other 2 groups (normals and patients with other brain lesions). The group of patients with brain lesions not involving the central part of the optic system also differed from the normal subjects in that all qualities of the optic stimulation syndrome were reduced, but more especially the occurrence of complex hallucinations and of dysmorphopsias and dysmegalopsias. This is probably related to the weakened action of psychotoKiirnetic agent:s in organic brain disease. Other investigations are briefly mentioned, in which similar reductions of the effect of psychotomimetics have been noted in relation to nonvisual hallucinations and disturbances of time sense. The cause of the reduction of the optic stimulatory effect of psilocybine in patients with central lesions of the optic system is sought in a (purely hypothetical) supramaximal inhibition (in the sense of Vvedenskis parabiosis), or in a weakening of facilitatory corticofugal activity in the presence of such lesions.

author_address: J.B. Appel, Dept of Psychiat., Univ. of Chicago, Chicago, IL, United States
note: (Appel, Freedman) Dept of Psychiat., Univ. of Chicago, Chicago, IL, United States
title: Tolerance and cross-tolerance among psychotomimetic drugs
abstract: A fixed ratio schedule of milk reinforcement (FR30) was used to study tolerance to the effects of D lysergide, L lysergide, bromciysergide, psilocybin, mescaline, and dexamphetamine in the rat A decrease in the amount of disruption of bar pressing occurs with repeated daily administration of appropriate doses of all the psychotomimetic compounds, and cross tolerance was also demonstrated.

note: (Hill, Fischer, Warshay) Coll. of Optom., Ohio State Univ., Columbus, OH, United States
title: Effects of excitatory and tranquilizing drugs on visual perception
abstract: Changes of spatial distortion threshold in response to the hallucinogen, psilocybin, were measured. A marked loss of compensation for optically induced distortions at drug peak was found. Compensation returned as the drug course elapsed.

author_address: W.F. Herblin, Sect. of Neurobiol. and Behav., Cornell Univ., Ithaca, NY, United States
note: (Herblin, O'Brien) Sect. of Neurobiol. and Behav., Cornell Univ., Ithaca, NY, United States
title: Interactions of norepinephrine with subcellular fractions of rat brain. L characteristics of norepinephrine uptake
abstract: The uptake of exogenous norepinephrine by subcellular fractions of rat brain has been investigated in a sucrose-NaCl-Trie buffer medium. Although the uptake of norepinephrine has been shown tobe a temperature-dependent process, these studies were run at 0-4degree C so that the results would be compatible with subsequent binding experiments. The uptake of this catecholamine which occurs at 0-4 C is inhibited by pyrogallol, bufotenin, and ergotamine and is activated by serotonin and psilocybin. Plots of norepinephrine uptake as a function of the equilibrium norepinephrine concentration have indicated that the uptake of norepinephrine is a multicomponent phenomenon, and this is supported by inhibition data. One component appears to be associated with the microsomal fraction and is inhibited by serotonin, pyrogallol, and ergotamine, and activated by psilocybin. A second component appears to be associated with nerve-ending particles and exhibits a very similar drug profile. A third component also appears to be associated with nerve-ending particles and isnhibited by ergotamine but activated by bufotenin, serotonin, and psilocybin.

author_address: A. Struyvenberg, Evans Mem. Dept. of Clin. Res., Univ. Hosp., Boston, MA, United States
note: (Struyvenberg, Morrison, Relman) Evans Mem. Dept. of Clin. Res., Univ. Hosp., Boston, MA, United States
title: Acid-base behavior of separated canine renal tubule cells
abstract: In separated canine renal tubules intracellular pH was calculated from the distribution of DMO-14C, using inulin as a measurement of noncellular water, At normal PCO2 and extracellular (HCO3-), renal cells were found to be more alkaline (mean pH 7.32) than most other mammalian cells. Cell acidity varied in direct linear relation to extracellular acidity when the latter was changed by systematic variation of either PCty or extracellular [HCO3-], but PCO2 had a significantly greater effect. Inhibition of carbonic anhydrase by addition of 10-3 M acetazolamide significantly increased cellular pH. Neither acute potassium depletion nor rapid repletion significantly affected cell pH. The results suggest that renal tubular cells are relatively alkaline because they secrete acid; the secretory process appears to be only indirectly linked to carbonic anhydrase.

tertiary_title: Soucasny vyskyt neurologickych priznaku a zmeneneho proprioceptivniho vnimani po psilocybinu u nemocnych s organickym poskozenim mozku

title: Simultaneous neurological signs and changes in proprioception after psilocybin in organic brain lesions
abstract: Motor signs and proprioceptive changes were shown to occur simultaneously after a standard single dose (0.15 mg/kg) of psilocybin in 96 patients with organic brain lesions of varying etiology and localization. The following neurological signs could be demonstrated: pronounced manifestations of pyramidal deficiency in central paresis; the presence of articulatory disorders and disorders of motor coordination and pronounced symbolic disorders, e.g., expressive aphasia, agraphia, apraxia and astereognosia.

tertiary_title: Etude comparative de l'action de la psilocybine sur les potentiels evoques au niveau du cortex occipital et d'une aire corticale specifique chez un Cercopitheclnae Papio papio
author_address: F. Bermond, Lab. de Neurobiol., Fac. de Medecine, Dakar
note: (Bermond, Bert, Ayats) Lab. de Neurobiol., Fac. de Medecine, Dakar
title: A comparative study of the effect of psilocybin on the evoked potentials in the occipital cortex and on a specific cortical area in Papio Papio (Cercopithecinae)
abstract: A study was made of the effect of psilocybin on 14 baboons (Papio papio). The potentials evoked by stimulation with light and sound were evaluated with computed averages (Enhancetron 1024). The potentials were derived from the occipital area and a nonspecific cortical area. Whereas the drug has a very marked effect on the visually evoked potential, it only causes a discrete change in the potentials evoked in a nonspecific area; a reduced amplitude was found, especially in the late waves. These changes are not attributable to habituation or to a change in the state of vigilance of the animal.

note: (Buck) Massachusetts Med. Soc., Boston, MA, United States
title: Psychedelic effect of pholiota spectabilis
abstract: P. spectabilis (Gymnopilus spectabilis) is a wellknown and recognizable wild mushroom that is generally considered inedible only because of its bitter taste, although attention has recently been called to it s hallucinogenic properties. Thin-layer chromatography of a methanol extract indicated the presence of indole derivatives, but there was no probable evidence of the presence of psilocinof psilocybin. (2C1 8B*).

author_address: S.J. Corne, Dept. of Pharmacol. Res., Parke-Davis and Co., Hounslow, United Kingdom
note: (Corne, Pickering) Dept. of Pharmacol. Res., Parke-Davis and Co., Hounslow, United Kingdom
title: A possible correlation between drug-induced hallucinations in man and a behavioural response in mice
abstract: The production of head twitches in mice appears to be a suitable laboratory test for predicting whether a compound is likely to be hallucinogenic in man. This is based on the following findings: With the exception of acetyllysergide and nalorphine, hallucinogenic drugs induced head twitches in mice. Chemically related compounds which are not hallucinogenic did not induce head twitches with the exception of 5-HTP, ergometrine, alpha-ethylmescaline and 3,4-dimethoxyphenethylamine (DMPE). It is suggested that these 4 drugs might produce hallucinations if they were given in high enough doses. There is a good correlation between drug-induced hallucinations in man and drug-induced head twitches in mice in terms of dose/kg. Chlorpromazine, haloperidol, tetrahydroaminacrine and MAO inhibitors can antagonize hallucinations in man. These same compounds antagonized head-twitches induced in mice by the appropriate hallucinogens. Cross-tolerance has been demonstrated between lysergide (LSD) and mescaline, LSD and psilocybin and LSD and DMT in man. Mescaline, psilocybin and DMT also antagonized LSD-induced head twitches in mice. A potent antiserotonin, methysergide, antagonized the head twitches induced by a wide variety of chemically different hallucinogens. This gives support to the idea that hallucinogens may act by mimicking, releasing or potentiating serotonin centrally.

author_address: E.T. Uyeno, Stanford Res. Inst., Menlo Park, CA, United States
note: (Uyeno) Stanford Res. Inst., Menlo Park, CA, United States
journal_name: Archives internationales de pharmacodynamie et de therapie
title: Effects of mescaltne and psilocybin on dominance behavior of the rat
abstract: Two dose-response experiments indicated that mescaline and psilocybin inhibited dominance behavior of rats competing for food. The times of peak inhibitory effects of mescaline and psilocybin are 30 min after the i. p. injection. The dose-response curves show that per cent inhibition of dominance behavior is an increasing function of dose. The ED of the mescaline curve is 4.02 mg/kg (3.14-5.15 mg/kg), and that of the psilocybin curve is 0.215 mg/kg (0.159-0.290 mg/kg).

note: (Ginestet) Clin. de la Fac. Med., Paris
title: The hallucinogenous substances
Effect of certain psychopharmacologic substances on S35-methionine cytoplasm incorporation (cyrillic)
abstract: The effect of certain psychopharmacologic substances on S35-methionine cytoplasmic incorporation was studied by autohistoradiographic technics. It was shown that the psychanaleptic methylphenidate increased incorporation of S35-methionine in the cytoplasm of the brain and liver cells (tests on rats) while the neuroleptic chlorpromazine decreased it. Centrophenoxine decreases the incorporation of labeled methionine in the cytoplasm of the liver cells (tests on mice). Serotonin also decreased the incorporation of S35-methionine in the liver cells and increased it in the cells of the renal convoluted tubules. The antiserotonin methysergide increased incorporation of S35-methionine in the cytoplasm of all organs tested (liver, spleen and kidney), while under the effect of the antiserotonin psilocybine this increase was observed only in the cytoplasm of the liver cells. The combined application of serotonin with methysergide or with psilocybine resulted in considerable balancing of the effect achieved by the isolated application of each of the substances in the incorporation of the marked amino acid (tests on mice).

author_address: C.E. Spooner, Brain Res. Inst., UCLA Cent. for the Hlth. Scis., Los Angeles, CA, United States
note: (Spooner, Winters) Brain Res. Inst., UCLA Cent. for the Hlth. Scis., Los Angeles, CA, United States
title: Neuropharmacological profile of the young chick
abstract: The EEG and behavioral effects of diverse centrally active pharmacological agents were studied in unrestrained, unanesthetized, 5-14 day old white Leghorn cockerels. Effective doses of the barbiturates, alpha-chloralose, chlorpromazine, reserpine, and morphine, produced behavioral depression and associated slow wave EEG activity. The hallucinogenic compounds, lysergic acid diethylamide, psilocybin, harmine, and mescaline, induced behavioral excitation, EEG arousal activity and abnormal body postures; the initial effects were often followed by behavioral depression. Caffeine produced no apparent alteration of either the EEG or the behavior of the young chick. Atropine induced an FEG arousal pattern, locomotor ataxia, and later a perceptible increase in normal motor activities. Amphetamine produced desynchronized EEG patterns characteristic of arousal, increased vocal activity, abnormal postures, and increased locomotor activities. Drug interactions with the unique amphetamine chick response revealed that atropine was the most effective amphetamine potentiating agent examined; while diphenhydramine and related agents were the most effective blocking agents of amphetamine induced behavior, that by themselves did not produce behavioral depression. Subconvulsant doses of metrazol produced slow wave EEG activity and behavioral quiescence; while convulsant doses induced clonus and diffuse, hight voltage, spiking waves in the EEG. Strychnine produced tonic convulsions while the EEG demonstrated only a desynchronized pattern and not a pattern of spikes. The few differences in drug responses between avian and mammalian species appeared to be related to the absence of an avian functional cerebral cortex and a neothalamo-cortical anatomical complex. These anatomical differences in the bird result in: the absence of myoclonic jerking following alpha-chloralose; the apparent lack of a caffeine stimulatory effect; the association of the atropine-induced EEG and behavioral effects; and the absence of strychnine-induced spikes in the cerebral hemisphere EEG. The many similarities in responsiveness between avian and mammalian species were more striking than the few differences. Especially prominent was the demonstration that the chick responses to those agents that effect mechanisms underlying the states of wakefulness and sleep, i.e. the barbiturates, chlorpromazine, reserpine, and amphetamine, were comparable to the responses reported for mammalian species. This suggested that there are a number of fundamental central nervous system mechanisms controlling EEG and behavioral activities, and originating in subcortical brain areas that appear to share common properties and presence in the homeothermal vertebrates.
